title: Hard Attend
subtitle: Score three items, pick the highest exactly, and read its value two ways that agree.

chapters.title: Closer Wins
chapters.blurb: A two-number key turns "which item is nearest the query?" into "which score is highest?".
captions: Three items sit on a line: Aster is worth ten, Banyan twenty, Cobalt thirty. A query lands somewhere near them, and you want the value of the nearest one.
This lab is a teaching page, plain web code rather than a numeric program. It turns that nearness question into scores, then picks exactly.
Give each item a key of two numbers: twice its position, and minus its position squared. Banyan, at position one, gets two and minus one.
The query is the pair query and one. Multiply the pairs and add, and the score is twice the query times the position, minus the position squared.
Park the query at one. Aster scores zero, Banyan scores one, Cobalt scores zero. Banyan is the tallest, and Banyan is the nearest.
Across the positions, that score is the query squared minus the squared distance to the query. So the scores trace a parabola that peaks at the query.
Slide the query down to zero. Aster takes the lead with zero, while Banyan falls to minus one and Cobalt to minus four.
Slide it up to two. Cobalt leads with four, Banyan has three, and Aster has zero.
In between, the curve slides smoothly. At one and a quarter, Banyan scores one and a half and Cobalt scores one, so Banyan is still nearest.
At exactly one half, Aster and Banyan are equally near, and both score zero. The scores alone cannot name a single winner there.
So scoring turns nearest into highest. Next comes the harder part: choosing one winner exactly, even when two scores tie.

chapters.title: One Winner, Two Reads
chapters.blurb: The first highest score wins, ties go left, and a one-hot sum and a direct index read return the same value.
captions: Scores are not an answer yet. You need one winner, the position of the highest score, a choice called argmax, plus a tie rule decided in advance.
The page walks the scores from left to right. It starts with the first item as the leader, then challenges that leader with each item after it.
A challenger takes over only if its score is strictly greater. Equal is not enough, so the earlier item keeps the lead.
At a query of one half, Banyan ties Aster at zero, fails to beat it, and Aster wins. Ties go left.
At one and a half, Banyan and Cobalt both score two. Banyan holds the lead against Cobalt, so Banyan wins.
Now read the winner's value. The first way is a one-hot list: a one at the winner's position and zeros everywhere else.
Multiply each bit by its item's value and add them up. With Banyan winning, zero, one, zero against ten, twenty, thirty gives twenty.
The second way skips the sum and reads the value at the winner's position directly. The page prints Banyan's twenty, and labels this read hard attend.
The two reads agree at every query. That is by construction, since both start from the same winner, so it checks the bookkeeping rather than discovering anything.
They differ in cost. The one-hot sum touches every item, while the toolkit's index read copies one entry in a single operation at any table size.
That is hard attention: score, take the leftmost highest, read the winner. It is exact, with no blending anywhere.

chapters.title: Soft Versus Exact
chapters.blurb: Softmax only approaches the exact read, never at a tie, and the scored-selection question stays open.
captions: The page adds a third read, softmax. It turns every score into a weight, the weights add up to one, and the value is the blend of all three items.
A sharpness slider scales the score gaps before the exponential, from one half up to fourteen. Turning it up makes the weights spikier.
At a query of one quarter and sharpness fourteen, Aster gets nearly all the weight. The blend is about ten point zero one: close to ten, never exactly ten.
At three quarters it flips toward Banyan. The blend is about nineteen point nine nine, near the exact answer of twenty but not equal to it.
Away from ties, more sharpness pulls the blend toward the exact value. At a tie it cannot: at one half, Aster and Banyan split the weight evenly at any sharpness, giving fifteen.
At one and a half, the same even split gives twenty-five where the exact rule gives twenty. Softmax averages ties; the exact rule picks the left.
That is the contrast. Softmax only approaches the exact read, and exact picking needs an explicit tie rule.
The folder has no tests, and the page needs a browser, so it cannot run in a terminal. It is a teaching sketch.
The old plan's indexed half, reading at a chosen position, is now covered by index reads. Gather lowering found hard attention after a selection was made, but learned no scoring.
The scored half, learning a shared scoring rule from changing data, stays open. The notes warn exact selection has no useful gradient, so training would go through soft mixtures.
So the journey: score by closeness, pick the leftmost highest, and read the value two agreeing ways. Whether a circuit can learn those scores is still an open question.
